raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old male was referred to our emergency department with acute onset abdominal pain of 12 h duration. Pain was associated with nausea and giddiness. Preliminary abdominal sonography done at the primary hospital showed presence of free fluid in the pelvis and left hypochondrium. The patient was shifted for computed tomography (CT) scan, where he collapsed, and test abandoned. He responded to fluid challenge and referred to higher centre for further management.
On admission, his pulse was 94/m with systolic blood pressure 90/60 mm, oxygen saturation of 90%. There was tenderness in left hypochondrium and periumbilical region but had no history or signs of external trauma. Intravenous fluids were given, and he was shifted for CT scan of the abdomen which revealed a 7 cm x 6 cm sub-capsular peri-splenic haematoma with moderate hemoperitoneum in peri-hepatic area, paracolic gutters and pelvis [Figure 1].
The patient was monitored in Intensive Care Unit, kept nil by mouth, started on intravenous antibiotics and analgesics. Blood investigations showed haemoglobin (Hb) of 14 g%, white blood cells of 15,400/cumm and platelet count of 280 x 1000/cumm with normal coagulation profile. Since there was no history of trauma, a detailed workup was done for the cause of splenic rupture, tests for typhoid, dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, infectious mononucleosis were negative.
Repeat Hb at 6 h showed a drop to 11 g%. Abdominal discomfort and pain persisted with features of localised guarding in the left hypochondrium. A repeat abdominal sonography showed an increase in the hemoperitoneum. Considering the persistent pain, drop in Hb and increasing hemoperitoneum, we subjected him for laparoscopic sos open surgical intervention. Supine with leg split and reverse Trendelenburg position was given. The camera port was trans-umbilical, and the port for liver retraction was also in the midline, at xiphisternum. Working ports were 5 mm midway between umbilicus and xiphisternum and 10 mm port in left periumbilical region, additional 5 mm in left anterior axillary line was made for splenic retraction. The operating surgeon stood between the legs, whereas camera surgeon on patient's right side and 2nd assistant on the left side. There was 1000cc of hemoperitoneum with clots in the perisplenic, perihepatic and pelvic region [Figure 2]. The spleen size and surface was normal except for a small capsular breach on the medial surface. There was no obvious parenchymal laceration or tear. The splenic vessels were normal. The liver and other abdominal organs were normal. After sucking out intraperitoneal blood and clots, continuous trickle of bright red ooze was evident from the medial surface of the splenic parenchyma. Hence, we proceeded for splenectomy. Ultrasonic scissors were used, and splenic hilum dissected. We continued in the same position since hilar anatomy was well-visualised. Splenic artery was ligated with 2/0 silk, clipped doubly and cut. Splenic vein too was tackled in similar manner and spleen was carefully dissected free off its attachments. Operation time was 90 min; umbilical port incision was extended and spleen delivered intact after placement in a retrieval bag. Drainage tube was placed in splenic fossa through 5 mm flank port, and umbilical incision was closed meticulously with non-absorbable sutures.
Post-operative course was uneventful. His Hb was 9.9 g%, started on orals on day 1, drain removed and discharged on day 3 with a good cosmetic scar [Figure 3]. He was vaccinated against encapsulated bacterial organisms. Histopathology of the spleen did not reveal any abnormality except some congestion of hilar vessels. There was no evidence of vasculitis. There was no parasitic infiltration of spleen or any pathological cause of splenic rupture. Patient is stable at 24 months follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male was referred to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of acute-onset abdominal pain associated with nausea and giddiness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute abdominal pain 12 hours prior to referral accompanied by nausea and giddiness, with no history of external trauma. At the primary hospital, abdominal ultrasonography showed free fluid in the pelvis and left hypochondrium; during an attempted CT scan, he suffered hemodynamic collapse requiring fluid resuscitation before transfer to our center.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of external trauma or prior medical illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute abdominal pain, nausea, giddiness, and syncope/collapse.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, pulse rate was 94/min, blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 90%. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the left hypochondrium and periumbilical region (later progressing to localized guarding in the left hypochondrium), with no external signs of trauma.
objective.routine_investigations: Preliminary outside ultrasound showed free fluid in the pelvis and left hypochondrium. Admission hemoglobin was 14 g% (dropping to 11 g% at 6 hours), WBC 15,400/cu.mm, platelets 280,000/cu.mm, and coagulation profile was normal. Repeat abdominal ultrasound at 6 hours showed increasing hemoperitoneum. Etiologic workup for atraumatic splenic rupture—including tests for typhoid fever, dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and infectious mononucleosis—was completely negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan demonstrated a 7 cm x 6 cm subcapsular perisplenic hematoma with moderate hemoperitoneum in the perihepatic space, paracolic gutters, and pelvis. Laparoscopic splenectomy evacuated 1,000 mL of intraperitoneal blood and clots and identified a small capsular breach on the medial splenic surface with active bright red oozing but normal splenic size, vessels, and parenchyma. Histopathology of the resected spleen showed only mild hilar vascular congestion without vasculitis, parasitic infiltration, or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Idiopathic (atraumatic) spontaneous splenic rupture with massive hemoperitoneum, confirmed by abdominal CT, diagnostic/therapeutic laparoscopy, and splenic histopathology after excluding typhoid fever, malaria, dengue, leptospirosis, infectious mononucleosis, and trauma. Due to persistent abdominal pain, falling hemoglobin (from 14 g% to 11 g%), and expanding hemoperitoneum, the patient underwent successful laparoscopic splenectomy (90-minute operative time). Postoperative recovery was uneventful (postoperative Hb 9.9 g%); he resumed oral intake on day 1, received vaccinations against encapsulated bacteria, and was discharged on postoperative day 3, remaining asymptomatic at 24-month follow-up.
